title: Peace in the home
hookLine: a high value in Jewish family life
last: THESE AND THESE: ARGUE HONESTLY, SHARE THE TABLE.

cards: Sarah is inside the tent, listening. Outside, a guest tells Abraham that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. She laughs to herself.

In the King James words, she says: "After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?" A verse later, God speaks to Abraham about that laugh and repeats what she said. Except the repeat is different.
Listen closely, because today's word hides in the part that goes missing.

teach.b: You met this page of Talmud in your first year; today, what it means for a home. When God tells Abraham what Sarah said, the King James has: "Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?" Sarah's age stays in.
Abraham's is gone. She had said, my lord is old too; God reports only, I am old. The Talmud notices and draws a lesson: great is peace, for even the Holy One altered words for its sake.
Nobody needs to carry every sharp word from one spouse to the other. Peace is also something you chase.
Hillel taught: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.
Tradition tells of Aaron going to each side of a quarrel separately, telling each how much the other regretted it, until they met and embraced. And it's small and daily.
The Talmud asks: if you can afford only one light, for Shabbat or for Hanukkah, which comes first?

teach.h: A LAMP SO WE CAN SEE.
teach.b: The Shabbat lamp in the home, for the sake of shalom bayit: a lit house, where nobody trips in the dark and tempers don't flare. Peace starts with being able to see each other.
Shalom bayit is not silence, and it's not keeping up appearances. Teachers of this value say clearly that it never asks anyone to stay where they are not safe.
It means a home where people are gentle on purpose, choose their words with care, and keep making the first move toward each other.

how: Jewish tradition counts shalom bayit, peace in the home, as a high value in family life; teachers draw on texts like God's softened report of Sarah's words and Hillel's call to love and pursue peace.

o: a blessing said when moving into a new house
keeping quiet at home so no one ever argues
peace in the home, pursued through small daily choices

s: God repeats Sarah's words to Abraham word for word
the part about Abraham's age is left out, and the Talmud says it was for peace.
the Talmud puts the Shabbat lamp before Hanukkah lights, for peace at home
if you can afford only one, the home's Shabbat light comes first.
shalom bayit means staying quiet about everything
it's not silence, and it never asks anyone to stay where they aren't safe.

games.q: Sarah laughed and said she was old, and that Abraham was old too. you're about to tell Abraham what she said. what do you say?
o: repeat every word, including the part about his age.
say only that she laughed because she is old.
tell him nothing about the laugh.
games.why: God reports only Sarah's own age; the Talmud learns from this that even the Holy One altered words for the sake of peace.

practice: Bring to mind the people you live with, or those closest to you, and one small friction between you right now: a sharp word, a chore, a silence gone on a little long.
Choose one small move toward peace, a kind word or a sharp sentence you decide not to pass along, and hold it until it feels doable.
And if home is ever not safe, please reach out: local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.

wordCard.voice: Shalom bayit: peace in the home. Pursued, not waited for, and built from small choices, like the words God left out for Sarah and Abraham. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace of the house, peace in the home.

carryVoice: Your line: peace at home. Somebody has to go after it first. Rest well.
